transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-10-22 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Alex Rivera (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood SRE); Jordan Park (HelioTech CTO), Samira Ocampo (HelioTech Lead ML Eng), Lee Tran (HelioTech Infra).

Summary (auto): quick sync on POC latency trends, microburst incidents over the last 48h, kernel selection plan for sequence length variance, and next steps for log exchange and deep dive.

[00:00] Maya Chen: ok everyone thanks for joining, um we'll kick off, jordan and team thanks for making time, rough agenda is quick run-through of the last 48h latency picture, microburst profile, then alex has some kernel proposals, then we decide next steps. sound good?

[00:20] Jordan Park: yep sounds good, we're mostly hoping to confirm whether those microbursts are infra-related or model/routing, and figure out if dedicated bursting will materially help.

[00:35] Alex Rivera: yeah hi all, i'll share my screen in a sec, um just quick note i pulled the 2h trace around the two worst incidents last night, they line up with a heavy bump in 512 token requests, so seqlen distribution shift is large here.

[00:50] Samira Ocampo: i saw that too, we had a campaign that generated a lot of longer prompt expansions; it was an edge case but it exposed something.

[01:05] Lee Tran: and infra wise, our autoscaler didn't spin up extra workers fast enough — we saw a short enqueuing period. but my read is there was also an increase in time to first token, which makes me suspect KV cache warmness / kernel path change.

[01:28] Alex Rivera: right, two things to call out. first: TTFT spikes correlate with kernel switches — e.g., we fell back from the optimized fused-attn kernel to a slower generic kernel at about t+17s because of sequence padding edge. second: streaming handshake stalls appear when the prefix KV cache miss rate increases above ~12%.

[01:52] Samira Ocampo: can you explain the kernel switch part again — sorry i missed that detail.

[02:05] Alex Rivera: sure. our runtime decides kernels based on batch seqlen distribution and alignment; when a few requests in a batch exceed 512 it sometimes forces a conservative kernel that is compatible but slower, and that transition induces a small compile/dispatch overhead — not a full recompile but a slightly different path that shows as a TTFT bump, especially in first-stream token.

[02:35] Jordan Park: ok so is that deterministic? we need to know if it's repeatable to justify a Dedicated config.

[02:47] Priya Singh: it's semi-deterministic — repeatable given the same load mix and batch policy. we can simulate by replaying the request histogram. i'll give a config that reproduces it locally.

[03:05] Maya Chen: alex, can you walk the team through your three kernel options? quick bullets.

[03:15] Alex Rivera: yeah quick bullets — Option A: prefer fused-attn path optimized for 256/512 that has best latency for typical chat flows but degrades on long tails; Option B: hybrid hedging — keep fused-attn for low seqlen but spawn a shadow micro-batch for >512 that runs on a quantized path, costs more but reduces worst-case TTFT; Option C: conservative generic kernel with highest predictability across 256-2048 seqlen but average latency higher.

[03:55] Samira Ocampo: hedging sounds attractive but i'm worried about cost. can you quantify the extra cost?

[04:08] Alex Rivera: hedging adds roughly 12-20% token CPU/GPU time for the traffic mix you shared, but it lowers the 95/99p TTFT by 30-40% in our sims. numbers depend on batch size and caching.

[04:32] Lee Tran: question — how does KV cache warmness factor? we saw stream stalls where first-byte is fine but then stream stalls at token ~40-60.

[04:45] Priya Singh: that is consistent with cache churn. when you have many different prefixes hitting the same shard, the KV cache eviction increases lookup misses; that shows up as a mid-stream stall when a different kernel path needs remote fills. recommended: increase per-shard cache memory or do smarter prefix coalescing.

[05:12] Samira Ocampo: could batching policy changes help? we currently set max_batch_latency at 12ms.

[05:22] Alex Rivera: yup, we can tweak max latency and batch size to avoid mixing long and short seqlens. e.g., separate queuing for >512 requests or use seqlen-aware batching. that helps avoid kernel falls.

[05:45] Jordan Park: concrete ask — what should we run on our side to isolate infra versus model/runtime?

[05:55] Maya Chen: i'll summarize — SE to share the microburst profiling spreadsheet with guidance on logs to collect. customer to run two replay tests: (1) 1-hour standard heavy tail with seqlen histogram you saw, (2) isolated 512/1024 bursts to see deterministic kernel switches. also provide request-level traces with timestamps and model variant.

[06:23] Samira Ocampo: ok we'll do that, we can instrument the replay with the header X-Helio-RunID so you can correlate.

[06:35] Alex Rivera: perfect. also note: if you move to Dedicated burst capacity, we can pin a kernel policy to avoid mid-batch switching because you get isolated GPUs and fewer cross-tenant coalescing, but there's a cost delta.

[06:55] Lee Tran: about Dedicated — our procurement is slow, and if this is only an occasional microburst we might prefer a runtime hedging approach on hosted first.

[07:08] Priya Singh: that's fair. hedging is a good middle ground: lower TTFT tails with moderate cost. we'll propose specific hedging config for your traffic pattern.

[07:25] Jordan Park: are there any security or SSO implications with Dedicated? we need to keep audit logs and KMS integration.

[07:35] Maya Chen: Dedicated supports customer KMS and audit log forwarding; those are in the SOW. we'll include SOC2 controls and SAML/SSO mapping. i'll attach the security checklist after this call.

[07:50] Samira Ocampo: good. returning to kernel tradeoffs — alex can you share the simulated 95/99 percentiles for each option?

[08:05] Alex Rivera: yes quick numbers from the sim: Option A (fused-attn preferred): p95 ~ 85ms, p99 ~ 320ms. Option B (hybrid hedging): p95 ~ 70ms, p99 ~ 180ms. Option C (conservative): p95 ~ 120ms, p99 ~ 200ms. these are for your campaign histogram; exact numbers vary. hedging cuts the long tail most effectively.

[08:38] Samira Ocampo: ok that's helpful. earlier tests showed TTFT spikes to 1s in worst case — these sims lower that but we need real test to validate.

[08:50] Alex Rivera: agreed, sims assume cache warmness level of 88%; if your cache churn is higher the p99 will be worse. that's why we need the microburst logs.

[09:05] Lee Tran: what about streaming buffer sizes? we saw some stalls were related to handshake timeouts in our client.

[09:16] Priya Singh: recommended handshake timeout increase from default 6s to 10s for streaming in unstable networked clients; also enable early-first-token flush so the client gets partial tokens quicker. that reduces perceived TTFT.

[09:38] Jordan Park: any known issues with the SDK we should patch?

[09:44] Maya Chen: there was a 0.7.3 SDK quirk with streaming backpressure on some Node versions; we pushed 0.7.4 last week with fixes. make sure your client libs are on >=0.7.4.

[09:58] Samira Ocampo: noted. can you put the recommended config in a single doc so our infra can apply it?

[10:06] Alex Rivera: yes i'll produce a short playbook: seqlen-aware batching settings, hedging kernel config, cache memory recommendations, and handshake timeout patches.

[10:25] Maya Chen: priya will you outline the Dedicated burst economics vs hedging cost delta? john — sorry jordan — priya will put the rough delta numbers so you can present to finance.

[10:38] Priya Singh: yes i'll include a table showing expected cost per 100k requests with and without hedging and with a 2x dedicated burst.

[10:49] Jordan Park: that will help. also quick question about model variants — if we fall back to a quantized model for hedging does quality degrade noticeably?

[10:59] Alex Rivera: for most chat prompts quality delta is minimal for 1-2 tokens, but for long-form generation you may see slight syntactic differences depending on quantization. we can run a small eval set of 50 prompts from your corpus to measure.

[11:18] Samira Ocampo: we'll provide a 50 prompt sample.

[11:25] Alex Rivera: great. action recap: i'll share microburst profiling spreadsheet and the playbook; samira will run the replay tests and upload logs; priya will prepare cost delta and config recommendations; maya will send SOW/security checklist.

[11:42] Lee Tran: timeline — we should get initial artifacts this week, run the tests by end of next week, then reconvene. good?

[11:52] Maya Chen: yes let's tentatively schedule follow-up 2026-10-29 for a 30-min status, and then kernel deep dive the week after if logs show deterministic switching. i'll send invites.

[12:06] Jordan Park: perfect. thanks all. small note — ModelCloud reached out offering a custom runtime; not sure if that's useful but wanted to flag.

[12:18] Maya Chen: thanks for flagging. we can include a competitive note in the follow-up doc.

[12:30] Samira Ocampo: one last thing — can you also include a sample trace with the X-Helio-RunID so we know what traces to attach?

[12:38] Alex Rivera: yes i'll include an example curl with headers and the exact fields we need.

[12:45] Maya Chen: ok wrapping, thanks everyone. i'll follow up with notes and the security pack.

[12:52] (meeting ends)

Notes: Transcript contains minor transcription artifacts (misheard acronyms, punctuation). References to 'fused-attn' kernel and 'hedging' are runtime terms used by Redwood SE team. Shared artifacts referenced in call: microburst profiling spreadsheet (link to be shared), hedging playbook doc (to be shared), SOW/security checklist (to be shared).
